title: What a Bond Is
objective: After this level you can explain how a bond works as a loan to a government or company.
summary: A bond is an IOU: you lend to an issuer that pays interest and returns the face value at maturity. Bondholders are paid before shareholders. Britain's War Loan ran from 1917 to 2015.

cards.headline: In 2015, Britain repaid money it borrowed in 1917 to fight World War I.
cards.body: By then more than 120,000 holders were still owed a share of it, and still collecting interest. The loan was a bond. So what exactly were they holding?

cards.headline: A bond is an IOU you can buy
cards.body: Buying a bond means lending money to whoever issued it: a government, a city or a company. In return they promise interest at a set rate, usually paid on a schedule such as every six months, and your original sum, the face value, back on a set date called maturity. Level 8 said your bank balance is the bank's IOU to you. A bond is an IOU with a price tag.

mascot.line: Stocks and bonds get mixed up. A stock makes you an owner; a bond makes you a lender.

cards.headline: Steadier than stocks, not risk-free
cards.body: Bonds can bring a predictable income and help offset jumpier stocks. But the issuer might fail to pay: that's a default. If a company goes bust, its bondholders are paid before its shareholders, who get whatever is left, which may be nothing. Selling early has a catch too. When interest rates rise, new bonds pay more, so an older, lower-paying bond may only sell at a discount.

cards.fact: Britain's War Loan had no end date, until the government picked one.
cards.context: In 1932, holders of the 5% War Loan from 1917 were persuaded to switch to a lower-paying 3½% bond with no fixed maturity. That let the government choose when to repay. It waited until 2015, when interest rates were exceptionally low, and paid off the £1.9 billion still outstanding.

cards.headline: Bonds: issued
learned: A bond is a loan to its issuer
It pays interest and returns face value at maturity
Issuers can default; bondholders are paid first

questions.prompt: When you buy a bond, what are you doing?

options.label: Opening a savings account
options.rationale: A bond is a loan to a government, city or company.

options.label: Paying next year's taxes early
options.rationale: Buyers lend money and are paid interest for it.

questions.explanation: A bond is an IOU: the buyer lends, and the issuer pays interest and returns the face value at maturity.

questions.prompt: Why could Britain choose to wait until 2015 to repay its 3½% War Loan?

options.label: Its holders had agreed to give up all interest
options.rationale: Holders kept collecting interest until repayment.

options.label: Bonds never have to be repaid at all
options.rationale: Most bonds have a maturity date when the face value is due.

options.label: The bond had no fixed maturity date
A court had frozen the debt since 1932
options.rationale: The 1932 change was a swap into a new bond, not a court order.

questions.explanation: The 1932 conversion created a bond with no fixed maturity, so the government chose when to repay: in 2015, when rates were exceptionally low.

questions.prompt: A company goes bankrupt. Compared with Level 33's shareholders, where do its bondholders stand?

options.label: They get paid only after shareholders
options.rationale: It's the reverse: lenders come before owners.

options.label: They're paid first; shareholders get what's left
Both groups always lose everything
options.rationale: Bondholders are paid first from whatever assets remain.

options.label: Both groups share the assets equally
options.rationale: The order is set: bondholders before shareholders.

questions.explanation: Bondholders are lenders and are paid first. Shareholders are owners and get whatever is left, which may be nothing.
